case_study_insert.main_stem: Marrowvale Organic Farms (MOF) is a private limited company in the agribusiness sector, growing and packing organic vegetables for regional supermarkets and veg-box subscribers. The business has a workforce of 42 and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership, with founder Priya Nandra consulting growers at weekly planning meetings. MOF plans to invest $720,000 in a new wash-and-grade packhouse with cold storage, financed by a $450,000 five-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $252,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.20 a unit and a selling price of $12.20, and currently produces 82,000 units a year, where each unit is a packed carton. MOF faces two problems: 9.5% of harvested crates are rejected at grading for blemishing, and absenteeism among packing staff has reached 8%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report - Q3 2025: MOF packed 19,600 cartons last quarter, of which 9.5% were rejected at grading for blemishing, up from 6.8% a year earlier. Organic veg-box complaints rose to 33 from 20 a month. Average delivery to the depot is 2.8 days. A survey of 500 subscribers found that 68% would pay up to $0.50 more for certified organic boxes and 57% choose farms with published waste-reduction plans. A trial of the new wash line on one bay cut rejected crates to 4.2% and reduced water use by 15%. A separate packaging trial showed recyclable cardboard boxes reduced transit bruising by 11% but added $0.12 to each box. A skills audit found 11 of 42 staff had not completed on-the-job training on the new grader; off-the-job training at the county college costs $780 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Marrowvale Organic Farms as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Agribusiness Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing for capital investment. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 6.5% from $12.60 to $13.42 an hour from April 2026, raising the cost of packing crews. (3) Organic compost and feed input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, while average retail prices for organic vegetables rose only 3.1% and consumer spending on organic veg boxes grew 2.4%.

questions.question_text: MOF plans to fund part of its $720,000 packhouse with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MOF of using retained profit instead of the bank loan to finance the investment.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge and no fixed repayment schedule, which matters because MOF must cover fixed costs of $252,000 a year from a contribution of only $7.00 a carton ($12.20 − $5.20). Interest on a $450,000 loan would be a commitment in every month, including months when a poor harvest pushes the 9.5% rejection rate higher; keeping that cash inside the business protects the seasonal wage bill and the spending needed to cut rejected crates.

Point 2: Using MOF's own $270,000 removes the lender's security and conditions, so no bank can claim rights over the new wash-and-grade packhouse or veto the cropping plans that Priya Nandra agrees with growers at weekly meetings. Control stays with the existing owners, which suits the flat, democratic structure. The cost is that $270,000 of reserves can no longer act as a buffer if 8% absenteeism disrupts packing or if organic input costs keep rising.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to MOF's costs, reserves and ownership.

questions.question_text: MOF wants to build demand for its certified organic veg boxes. Consider advertising in organic trade magazines, hosting farmers' market tastings, or running a social media campaign for subscribers. Which should MOF choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Organic trade magazines: A technical advert reaches supermarket produce buyers and wholesale decision-makers, and it can carry the evidence buyers now demand, such as the wash-line trial that cut rejected crates from 9.5% to 4.2%. Readership is small, and the message does not reach the 500 subscribers among whom 68% would pay $0.50 more.

Farmers' market tastings: Sampling at markets lets shoppers taste the vegetables and builds local loyalty, which supports the 57% who choose farms with waste-reduction plans. It is cheap and gives instant feedback, but each event reaches only a few hundred people, lasts a day, and is slow to grow the 19,600 cartons packed each quarter, so the link to the $720,000 packhouse is weak.

Social media campaign: A subscriber-facing campaign can show harvests, the wash line and recyclable cardboard boxes at low cost per view, with results measured click by click. It converts the 68% willing to pay $0.50 more into actual premium sales and reinforces the 2.8-day delivery story. It demands constant content and cannot present detailed quality evidence to supermarket buyers.

Recommendation: MOF should choose the social media campaign, supported by occasional market tastings. It targets the subscribers already identified in the survey, scales beyond a single market and costs far less than magazine advertising while the $450,000 loan is being serviced. Trade magazines are rejected because they miss the subscribers who will pay the premium, and market tastings are rejected as too small and short-lived to fill a packhouse built for 82,000 cartons a year.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to MOF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MOF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade magazines and market tastings are rejected.

questions.question_text: MOF's absence rate has reached 8% and grading rejections stand at 9.5%. Explain two benefits for MOF of its democratic leadership style in tackling these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the workforce of 42 speak at the weekly planning meetings Priya Nandra chairs, so packers can explain why crates are being blemished and suggest gentler handling before the wash line is installed. Because staff help decide how grading is organised, they are more committed to hitting the 4.2% rejection rate achieved on the trial bay, protecting the 19,600 cartons packed each quarter and the supermarket contracts behind the $720,000 investment.

Point 2: Consulting the team about shift patterns addresses the 8% absenteeism directly, because the people who experience the workload can propose realistic rotas rather than having changes imposed. Better attendance means the new grader is operated by experienced staff, cutting the 33 monthly complaints and protecting the $12.20 price and $7.00 contribution. Involvement also supports the flat structure: growers and packers who are heard are more likely to stay, even while the packhouse construction disrupts the site.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to MOF's absence rate, rejection rate, output and leadership.

questions.question_text: MOF must train 11 of 42 staff to operate the new grader. Consider on-the-job training on the packhouse line or off-the-job training at the county college. Which should MOF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching beside the new grader teaches MOF's own settings, grading standards and cleaning routines, costs no course fees, and keeps the 11 trainees productive while 19,600 cartons a quarter must still be packed. It can attack the 9.5% rejection rate immediately because supervisors correct mistakes on real crates. The drawbacks are that experienced packers lose time teaching, bad habits may be copied, and there is no external certificate to prove competence to supermarket auditors.

Off-the-job training: The county college course costs $780 per employee, so 11 × $780 = $8,580, a modest sum beside the $720,000 packhouse. It gives structured teaching and a recognised certificate, useful as MOF seeks the 57% of shoppers who favour farms with published plans. However, it withdraws 11 of 42 staff from the line during harvesting, risking the 2.8-day delivery promise, and the generic content still needs adapting to MOF's own equipment.

Decision: MOF should choose on-the-job training first, with a short college module later for the supervisors. It is cheaper, specific to the installed grader and avoids losing packing capacity while 8% absenteeism is already thinning the team. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because the $8,580 fee and the lost shifts would slow the 19,600-carton operation and cannot directly cut the 9.5% rejection rate. A pilot on one bay should be checked against the 4.2% trial figure before the $780 per head is spent on everyone. Priya Nandra should also check that 8% absenteeism has eased, because sending staff to college while shifts are short of hands would leave the 19,600-carton target at risk.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MOF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of MOF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to the new grader.

questions.question_text: MOF's management wants to use its cost and output data to plan the new packhouse. Calculate and explain how that data can be used.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $252,000 ÷ ($12.20 − $5.20) = $252,000 ÷ $7.00 = 36,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 36,000 cartons a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.20 − $5.20 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MOF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. With break-even at 36,000 cartons and output of 82,000, MOF has a margin of safety of 46,000 cartons, so even a season badly hit by the 9.5% rejection rate would still cover the $252,000 fixed costs.
2. Contribution of $7.00 lets managers test the survey result that 68% of subscribers would pay $0.50 more: that premium lifts contribution to $7.50 and could fund the $450,000 loan faster, if the extra price is accepted.
3. Average total cost of $8.27 a carton ($252,000 ÷ 82,000 = $3.07, plus $5.20) gives a benchmark for the new packhouse: washing and grading must cut rejections below 9.5% or raise output for the $720,000 investment to reduce unit cost.
4. The same figures help judge financing: the $270,000 retained profit leaves 46,000 cartons of cushion before losses, so managers can assess whether interest on the $450,000 loan is affordable while the 8% absence rate is being tackled.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 36,000 cartons | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 46,000-carton margin of safety against the 9.5% rejection rate; a $0.50 premium lifting $7.00 contribution; an $8.27 unit-cost benchmark for the packhouse; and loan affordability against retained profit.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MOF's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MOF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.36 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.66 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.20 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $96,000 inventories + $132,000 trade receivables + $44,000 cash = $272,000, and 2025 current assets = $88,000 + $158,000 + $70,000 = $316,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives $272,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.36 and $316,000 ÷ $190,000 = 1.66. Excluding inventories: ($272,000 − $96,000) ÷ $200,000 = $176,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.88, and ($316,000 − $88,000) ÷ $190,000 = $228,000 ÷ $190,000 = 1.20.

Evaluation: Short-term liquidity strengthened on both measures. Current liabilities fell from $200,000 to $190,000 while current assets rose from $272,000 to $316,000, helped by cash doubling from $44,000 to $70,000. The stricter test, which strips out stock that may be rejected for blemishing, moved from 0.88 to 1.20, so MOF can now meet every short-term debt from cash and receivables alone rather than relying on selling crates. That matters while the cooperative of growers commits $270,000 of reserves and takes on a $450,000 loan for the $720,000 packhouse. Two cautions remain: receivables rose from $132,000 to $158,000, so subscribers and supermarkets are holding more of MOF's cash, and inventories fell from $96,000 to $88,000, which may reflect the 9.5% rejection problem rather than better stock control.

Conclusion: MOF's financial position has improved. Both measures rose, and the 1.20 figure shows the gain does not depend on unsold stock. The main risk is the growing receivables balance, so Priya Nandra should tighten credit terms before drawing further on the $450,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MOF of switching its veg boxes to recyclable cardboard packaging.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The packaging trial showed recyclable cardboard boxes cut transit bruising by 11%, which directly attacks the 9.5% rejection rate and helps MOF honour the 2.8-day delivery promise to subscribers. It also answers the 57% of surveyed shoppers who choose farms with published waste-reduction plans, supporting the $12.20 price and making the $720,000 packhouse easier to justify to supermarket buyers.

Disadvantage: The trial found cardboard added $0.12 to each box, which raises the $5.20 variable cost a unit and cuts contribution below $7.00 unless the full $0.50 premium is accepted by all 500 surveyed subscribers. Cardboard also weakens when wet, so condensation in chilled delivery could lift rejection back towards 9.5% and add to the 33 monthly complaints. The insert gives no figure for how many buyers would actually switch, so the net gain cannot be quantified and must be judged qualitatively with a small trial first. Priya Nandra should compare bruising and complaints during a limited launch with the current 2.8-day delivery record before converting the whole range.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to MOF's trial results, rejection rate, costs and survey.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in organic input costs will affect MOF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If the $450,000 five-year loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point increase adds 0.75% × $450,000 = $3,375 a year to interest. That is modest beside $252,000 of fixed costs, and MOF could fix the rate before drawdown, so the direct effect is containable. The indirect effect matters more: dearer credit makes the $720,000 packhouse harder to refinance if the build overruns, and it raises the cost of using the remaining $270,000 of reserves.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, from $12.60 to $13.42): Each packing hour costs $0.82 more (6.5% × $12.60 = $0.819). The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so no annual wage total can be calculated honestly; what can be judged is that with 8% absenteeism MOF reallocates shifts constantly, and unless productivity holds near 82,000 cartons from a workforce of 42, unit labour cost rises and the $7.00 contribution erodes.

Organic input costs (up 9.8%): These feed the $5.20 variable cost on every carton. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a labelled upper bound is defensible: if the entire $5.20 were exposed, 9.8% × $5.20 = $0.51 a carton, and at 82,000 cartons that is roughly $41,800 a year (82,000 × $0.5096). Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $7.00 contribution on each carton, and it recurs on every unit, unlike the one-off interest estimate. Retail organic prices rose only 3.1%, so much of it cannot be passed on.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in organic input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 82,000 cartons and directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that funds the $450,000 loan and the $720,000 packhouse, while the interest rise costs only $3,375 a year and can be capped by fixing the rate. The wage rise is second because it recurs with every shift, but productivity can absorb part of it. MOF should cut the 9.8% exposure through waste reduction and seek the $0.50 premium rather than absorb every increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to MOF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on MOF's costs, prices or finance in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that organic input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
